The city hired a man to remove the names from benches.

Not the plaques. Those remained: small rectangles of brass attached with screws that resisted rain, frost, and the occasional determined child. His job was to remove the names themselves.

The council had discovered that people were reluctant to sit on benches dedicated to strangers. They felt watched, or indebted, or vaguely as though they had entered someone else’s living room.

“It’s a utilization issue,” his supervisor explained.

The man’s name was Ellis. He had previously repaired clocks at the railway station, until the clocks were replaced by screens.

He was given a bicycle, a box of tools, and a map.

On Monday, he removed **MARGARET BELL, WHO LOVED THIS VIEW**.

The view was a duck pond containing no ducks and one orange traffic cone. Ellis stood there for a while before beginning. Then he knelt, applied the solvent, and worked the letters away with a soft cloth.

The brass beneath was brighter.

By lunchtime, Margaret Bell had become **WHO LOVED THIS VIEW**.

By two, there was only the view.

***

At home, Ellis kept the names in a notebook.

He wasn’t required to. The council maintained a spreadsheet, but its records contained only bench numbers, locations, and dates of completion.

His notebook contained other things.

**Arthur Singh. Beloved husband. Bench facing bakery.**

**Nina and Jo. Forty-three happy years. Broken slat.**

**For Daniel, who always stopped here. Nothing nearby.**

He found that last one troubling.

Nothing nearby: no river, no garden, no playground. Just a stretch of pavement between a pharmacy and a shuttered travel agency.

He sat on Daniel’s bench after finishing it.

People passed carrying groceries. A bus sighed at the curb. In the upstairs window of the pharmacy, someone watered a plant.

Ellis stayed until five.

***

On Thursday, a woman caught him removing her father.

“Excuse me,” she said.

Ellis lifted the cloth from the plaque.

She was wearing running clothes and holding a leash. At the other end stood a dog with the cautious expression of a retired accountant.

“That’s my father.”

Ellis looked down.

**PETER VALE, 1941–2018. HE MADE THINGS GROW.**

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“What are you doing?”

He explained the utilization issue.

The woman listened without interrupting. The dog sat.

When Ellis finished, she said, “He was terrible at gardening.”

Ellis glanced at the plaque again.

“Killed everything. My mother wrote that. She meant people, I suppose.”

“I haven’t started the name yet.”

The woman looked toward the trees.

“He used to bring sandwiches here. Egg sandwiches, even in hot weather. We told him it was dangerous.”

Ellis waited.

“He never listened.”

She laughed once, then tightened her grip on the leash.

“Do you have to do it today?”

“No,” Ellis said.

This was not strictly true, but he could make it true by going somewhere else.

***

That evening, he turned to a fresh page.

**Peter Vale. Egg sandwiches.**

He considered adding the gardening, but decided against it.

***

By the third week, Ellis had begun taking longer routes.

He arrived at benches when people were likely to be sitting on them. If a bench was occupied, he was permitted to postpone the work.

He became knowledgeable about lunch breaks, school dismissals, and the movements of dog walkers.

He learned that the bench outside the library belonged, in practice, to a young man who cried into his phone every Tuesday.

He learned that the one near the tennis courts supported three women who brought folding cushions and spoke about their husbands with immense, affectionate contempt.

He learned that Daniel’s bench caught the last direct sunlight in the neighborhood.

At four forty-seven, light slipped between the pharmacy and the travel agency and warmed the wood for eleven minutes.

Ellis timed it.

He still had his old watch.

***

His supervisor called him in.

“You’re falling behind.”

“Yes.”

“Is there a problem with the materials?”

“No.”

“The equipment?”

“No.”

The supervisor rotated a pen between her fingers.

Ellis noticed that her office contained no photographs. On the windowsill stood a cactus so brown it might have been made of paper.

“Do you ever sit outside?” he asked.

“Sometimes.”

“Where?”

She stopped turning the pen.

“What does that have to do with anything?”

“Nothing,” Ellis said.

She sighed and gave him until Friday to catch up.

***

On Friday morning, Ellis returned to Margaret Bell’s bench.

The pond had ducks now. The cone remained.

He opened his notebook, then his toolbox.

The letter punches were his own. He had used them years ago to mark replacement clock parts. He arranged them on the cloth beside him.

He couldn’t restore all the lettering. The punches were too large, and the polished area too narrow.

He chose a place along the bottom edge of the plaque and tapped carefully with his hammer.

**MARGARET.**

It took longer than he expected. The G was crooked.

At the next bench, he added **ARTHUR**.

At the next, **NINA + JO**.

By Daniel’s bench, his supervisor was calling. He let the phone ring.

He had finished the name and was putting away the punches when an old woman stopped beside him.

“Is the paint wet?”

“No paint.”

“Can I sit?”

“Of course.”

She lowered herself onto the bench with both hands braced against the wood. Ellis moved his toolbox.

For a while they watched the pharmacy window.

Then the sunlight arrived.

The woman closed her eyes.

“Oh,” she said. “That’s nice.”

Ellis sat beside her, his notebook open on his knee, and did not write anything down.
